section: What is a climate data cube?
text:
What is a climate data cube?


A data cube organises data along shared dimensions. For climate/EO variables, typically:
variable(time, latitude, longitude)


Harmonised: one grid, one calendar, consistent units and metadata.
Analysis-ready: select by label (time="2015-06-15"), not by file.
Not a file format: the organisation is the cube; here NetCDF is the input and Zarr the storage.

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
Why are we here?


Climate products are useful, but files arrive with different grids, time steps, packing, metadata and quality flags.




Today we build one small, transparent path from EUMETSAT LSA SAF files to a regional data cube.




Every step leaves an output you can open and check — and every choice is written down.

section: Where a cube fits in the ecosystem
text:
Where a cube fits in the ecosystem





STAC


Describe Standardise metadata for discovering geospatial assets.





Microsoft Planetary Computer


Discover and process Access open datasets through STAC and use hosted compute.





Google Earth Engine


Analyse Use a managed platform for large-scale geospatial analysis.





Zarr


Store Save chunked, compressed multidimensional arrays.





Xarray


Work with data Select, transform and analyse labelled arrays in Python.



STAC describes and helps discover assets; it is not a data cube format. Planetary Computer and Earth Engine are hosted platforms. Zarr is a storage format, Xarray a Python library.

Step 1 · Download
JOBS=8 bash code/01_download_sample.sh 2015 06 MDFVC \
  "https://datalsasaf.lsasvcs.ipma.pt/PRODUCTS/MSG/MDFVC/NETCDF"


2015-06: 30 file(s) on server, 30 to download -> data/raw/MDFVC/2015/06


First file: ~6s. Estimated remaining: ~0m22s with 8 parallel jobs


Done: 30 file(s) in 0m29s



JOBS = parallel downloads. Re-run any time: existing files are skipped, failed ones retried.

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
Download · inside the script
ENV_FILE="${ENV_FILE:-$PWD/code/.env}"
set -a; . "$ENV_FILE"; set +a
WGETRC="$(mktemp)"; export WGETRC; trap 'rm -f "$WGETRC"' EXIT
printf 'http_user=%s\nhttp_password=%s\n' "$LSASAF_USERNAME" "$LSASAF_PASSWORD" > "$WGETRC"

for d in $(seq -w 1 31); do                         # list every day folder of the month
  list+=$(wget -q -O- "$SRC/$YEAR/$MONTH/$d/" | grep -E '\.nc$' …)
done

get() { wget -q -O "$f.part" "$1" && mv "$f.part" "$f"; }    # .part → rename when complete
t0=$SECONDS; get "$(head -n1 <<< "$pending")" "$DEST"        # time one file → estimate
tail -n +2 <<< "$pending" | xargs -P "$JOBS" -I{} bash -c 'get "$1" "$2"' _ {} "$DEST"

Simplified excerpt; the real script adds retries, timeouts and reports failures. Walk through with the arrow keys: credentials → listing → safe download → parallel.

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
Processing · one file’s journey
cdo -sellonlatbox,$W,$E,$S,$N          in.nc    clip.nc        # crop (+ buffer)
cdo -delname,$QA_CSV                   clip.nc  main.nc        # continuous variables
cdo -selname,$QA_CSV                   clip.nc  qa.nc          # flags
cdo -remapbil,grid.txt                 main.nc  main_r.nc      # smooth → bilinear
cdo -remapnn,grid.txt                  qa.nc    qa_r.nc        # codes → nearest, never averaged
cdo merge main_r.nc qa_r.nc merged.nc                          # back together
cdo -s sinfo merged.nc && mv merged.nc out.part && mv out.part out_processed.nc  # only valid output lands

processing.parallel files run at once through xargs -P; results and failures go to data/interim/METREF/cdo.log.

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
Resampling is a decision








Method
Typical use
Main trade-off




Bilinear
Continuous fields (ETo, temperature, FVC)
Smooths; can shrink extremes


Nearest neighbour
Categories, QA flags
Preserves classes; looks blocky




Neither creates finer detail than the source. Choose per product, keep the QA flags, and record the choice.


✅ Checkpoint: one *_processed.nc per raw file · no status=failed in cdo.log · cdo sinfo shows the grid.txt size

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
Chunks · shards · compression
PROFILES = {   # inner chunk                              shard
  "map":        ({"time": 1,  "lat": 256, "lon": 256}, {"time": 10,  "lat": 512, "lon": 512}),
  "balanced":   ({"time": 8,  "lat": 128, "lon": 128}, {"time": 32,  "lat": 512, "lon": 512}),
  "timeseries": ({"time": 64, "lat": 32,  "lon": 32},  {"time": 256, "lat": 256, "lon": 256}),
}

c = min(inner[dim], size)                          # clamp chunk to the data
k = min(round(shard[dim] / c), ceil(size / c))     # shard = whole number of chunks
inner[dim], shard[dim] = c, c * k                  # (Zarr v3 sharding requires this)

ds = ds.chunk(shard)                               # one Dask task = one whole shard
encoding[var] = {"chunks": inner, "shards": shard,
                 "compressors": [BloscCodec(cname="zstd", clevel=5, shuffle="shuffle")]}
ds.to_zarr(tmp, zarr_format=3, encoding=encoding, consolidated=True)

The rounding fixes a real failure: a 300 × 400 AOI with 256-cell chunks and 512 shards would otherwise produce a shard that is not divisible by the chunk and Zarr refuses to write.

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
QA · what should we check?

Source vs output: coordinates, timestamps, units, variable names.
Decoded fill values and valid-cell fraction — per date, not just overall.
Missing-data footprint vs the product mask and QA flags.
A few known values and summary statistics, raw → interim → cube.


A file that opens is not automatically fit for analysis.

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
Caveats and uncertainty

Missing values may be real masks/QA exclusions — or configuration problems.
A crop/grid mismatch, wrong variable or undecoded fill value can create extensive NaNs.
Bilinear smooths; nearest is blocky. Different choices change statistics.
Degree grids have latitude-dependent ground size.
Product versions, temporal support, units and QA systems differ.
This is a teaching workflow, not a validated operational product.

title: Climate Data Cubes
section: On-the-fly processing vs a pre-built cube
text:
On-the-fly processing vs a pre-built cube









On-the-fly (catalog + lazy loading)
Pre-built cube (this tutorial)




Regridding
At read time; settings easy to overlook
Fixed once and documented


Compute cost
Paid at every query
Paid once, up front


Storage
Reuses the provider’s data
Creates a derived copy


Change area/grid/method
Change the query
Re-run the pipeline


Provider updates
Automatic
--append / rebuild



Neither is better in general — choose by use case and always record the resampling choice.

title: Climate Data Cubes
text:
Scale the pilot carefully

Benchmark a representative subset: runtime, peak memory, size, valid coverage, read speed of your real queries.
Grow in time batches with --append; split very large areas into grid-aligned tiles with a remap margin.
Parallelise within measured CPU, memory and disk limits (processing.parallel, JOBS, --workers).
Choose the chunk profile for the dominant question; re-benchmark at scale.


Do not scale only by adding workers — disk throughput, memory and object counts become the bottleneck.

text:
3 · 3_application.ipynb — climate and mobility
All figures come from code/plot_utils/adaptive_cube_plot.py:
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "code/plot_utils")
from adaptive_cube_plot import plot_time_slices, plot_spatial_timeseries, plot_climate_mobility_period

ds = xr.open_zarr("data/zarr/metref_cube.zarr")

1plot_time_slices(ds, var="METREF", time_index=[0, 14, 29],
                 boundaries=units, robust=True, ncols=3)

2plot_spatial_timeseries(ds, var="METREF",
                        points={"Dakar": (-17.19, 14.75)},
                        areas={"Whole cube": (-17.3, -11.2, 12.2, 16.8)},
                        show_area_spread=True)

3plot_climate_mobility_period(ds, mobility=mob, spatial_units=units,
                             var="METREF", period="2015-06-01", period_col="date",
                             mobility_metric="rate_depart", spatial_id_col="norm_id")

1

Panel maps on a regional Lambert Conformal projection with coastlines, borders, zone outlines and one shared colour bar.

2

Nearest-cell point series and area means with ±1 SD shading.

3

Half-month climate mean next to departures aggregated by origin zone.


What the notebook walks through:


Load the cube and the 151 zones (data/aoi/spatial_units_with_lat_lon.parquet, WKB geometry → GeoDataFrame).


Daily maps for the first, middle and last day with zone boundaries.


Half-month cumulative ETo (days 1–15 / 16–end, matching the mobility periods) — the aggregated DataArray goes straight into plot_time_slices.


Time series at three zone centroids and for two areas.


Zonal statistics without extra dependencies: every grid cell is assigned to a zone once (shapely.STRtree point-in-polygon), then one groupby reduces all time steps.


Climate ↔︎ mobility. Only one half-month of the ~17 M-row mobility table is read, using Parquet filters= (predicate push-down), then plotted side by side with the climate map.


Co-occurrence classes per zone: high/low ETo × high/low departures — a descriptive map, not a causal claim.








ImportantMatch the periods



The mobility data cover Feb 2013 – Dec 2015. For the climate–mobility steps, build a cube inside that window, e.g. bash code/01_download_sample.sh 2015 06 METREF → preprocess → build. With another period the maps and time series still run and the notebook tells you the mobility part was skipped.








The first Cartopy map downloads Natural Earth coastlines and borders (internet needed once, then cached).

code/.env is loaded after environment variables, so URL=… bash code/01_download_sample.sh is overwritten by the URL line in .env. Override the month, product and URL with arguments.





Example output
2015-06: 30 file(s) on server, 30 to download -> …/data/raw/METREF/2015/06
First file: ~6s. Estimated remaining: ~0m44s with 4 parallel jobs
Done: 30 file(s) in 0m52s
Re-running is safe: files that already exist are skipped and only failed ones are retried.






NoteWalk through the download script







code/01_download_sample.sh (simplified)

ENV_FILE="${ENV_FILE:-$PWD/code/.env}"
1set -a; . "$ENV_FILE"; set +a
WGETRC="$(mktemp)"; trap 'rm -f "$WGETRC"' EXIT
2printf 'http_user=%s\nhttp_password=%s\n' "$LSASAF_USERNAME" "$LSASAF_PASSWORD" > "$WGETRC"

3for d in $(seq -w 1 31); do
  list+=$(wget -q -O- "$SRC/$YEAR/$MONTH/$d/" | grep -E '\.nc$' …)
done

4get() { wget -q -O "$f.part" "$1" && mv "$f.part" "$f"; }
5xargs -P "$JOBS" -I{} bash -c 'get "$1" "$2"' _ {} "$DEST"


1

Credentials and defaults come from the private .env, never from the repository.

2

wget reads the password from a temporary file that is deleted on exit — it never appears in the process list.

3

Each day folder of the month is listed; days that do not exist return nothing.

4

Files are written as .part and renamed only when complete — an interrupted run never leaves a “finished-looking” half file.

5

JOBS downloads run in parallel.

title: B · Download and preprocess
text:
2 · Inspect a raw file
Never remap blind. Pick one file and look at variable names, grid and values:
f=$(ls data/raw/METREF/2015/06/*.nc | head -n1); echo "$f"
cdo -s showname      "$f"   # variable names → MAIN_VARIABLE and QA_VARIABLES
cdo -s sinfo         "$f"   # grid: lon/lat range and step, data type
cdo -s showtimestamp "$f"   # time stamp
cdo -s infon         "$f"   # min / mean / max per variable and number of missing values






TipCheck yourself




showname lists the product variable (e.g. METREF) and a QA variable (e.g. quality_flag).
sinfo shows a regular lonlat grid (for MSG-disk products e.g. -80 to 80 by 0.05).
infon shows plausible values for the product (METREF: mm/day, roughly 0–15).

title: B · Download and preprocess
text:
3 · Define the region
The region can come from the YAML bounds or from a vector file. Either way the script snaps it outward to whole raw-grid cells and writes the target grid to code/preprocess_utils/grid.txt.

Bounding box in YAMLVector AOI file


Edit code/preprocess_utils/config_resolution.yaml:


code/preprocess_utils/config_resolution.yaml

1domain:
  lon_min: -17.275
  lon_max: -11.225
  lat_min: 12.225
  lat_max: 16.775
processing:
2  parallel: 4
3  remap_method: bilinear
4  buffer: 0.2


1

Degrees (EPSG:4326). Snapped outward to raw cell edges on each run.

2

Files processed at the same time. This is the only place to set parallelism for preprocessing — an environment variable PARALLEL= is ignored.

3

bilinear for continuous fields, nearest for categorical ones. Applies to all non-QA variables; QA variables always use nearest neighbour.

4

Extra degrees cropped around the grid, so bilinear interpolation has real neighbours at the AOI edge.




Pass any GeoPandas-readable file (.shp, .gpkg, .geojson, .parquet) as the 4th argument (or AOI_FILE=). Its total bounds become the domain:
MAIN_VARIABLE=METREF uv run bash code/02_preprocess_cdo.sh \
  0.05 data/raw/METREF data/interim/METREF data/aoi/spatial_units.geosjon
If the file has no CRS, add AOI_CRS=EPSG:xxxx. The snapped rectangle is saved as data/interim/METREF/aoi_aligned.gpkg (change with AOI_OUTPUT=).









ImportantThe script updates the YAML in place



Each run rewrites the domain: and grid: sections of config_resolution.yaml with the snapped bounds (and with the AOI bounds when you pass a vector file). Commit or copy the file if you want to keep the previous region; restore the repository default with git checkout code/preprocess_utils/config_resolution.yaml code/preprocess_utils/grid.txt.

title: B · Download and preprocess
text:
4 · Crop and remap

Run it
1export MAIN_VARIABLE=METREF
2export QA_VARIABLES=quality_flag
3uv run bash code/02_preprocess_cdo.sh 0.05 data/raw/METREF data/interim/METREF

1

Required. Must match a name from cdo showname; the script stops and lists the available names otherwise.

2

Comma-separated QA/flag variables, remapped with nearest neighbour so flag codes are never averaged. Default quality_flag; every name must exist in the file.

3

uv run makes python3 inside the script use the project environment (YAML + grid helper). Arguments: resolution label (written to the log — the target grid always follows the raw grid’s cell size, 0.05° for MSG, so no false detail is created), input folder (searched recursively for *.nc) and output folder (use one folder per product so the cube builder never mixes products).

Aligned bounds: lon -17.275 to -11.225, lat 12.225 to 16.775

cdo    remapbil: Bilinear weights from lonlat (129x97) to lonlat (121x91) grid, with source mask (…)
cdo    remapnn: Nearest neighbor weights from lonlat (129x97) to lonlat (121x91) grid
…

NoteWalk through one file’s journey (process_cdo)







code/02_preprocess_cdo.sh (per file)

1cdo -sellonlatbox,$CLIP_WEST,$CLIP_EAST,$CLIP_SOUTH,$CLIP_NORTH  in.nc  clip.nc
2cdo -delname,$QA_CSV  clip.nc  main.nc
cdo -selname,$QA_CSV  clip.nc  qa.nc
3cdo -remapbil,grid.txt  main.nc  main_remap.nc
4cdo -remapnn,grid.txt   qa.nc    qa_remap.nc
5cdo merge main_remap.nc qa_remap.nc merged.nc
6cdo -s sinfo merged.nc && mv merged.nc out.nc.part && mv out.nc.part out_processed.nc


1

Crop to the target grid plus the buffer, so interpolation at the edge has neighbours.

2

Split continuous variables from QA flags.

3

Continuous variables: bilinear (or nearest, from the YAML).

4

Flags: always nearest neighbour — a flag value is a code, not a number to average.

5

Put them back together.

6

Only a readable result is renamed into place; temp files are removed on any failure. Existing valid outputs are skipped, so re-running resumes.

text:
5 · Check the output
ls data/interim/METREF/2015/06 | head -n3
tail -n 3 data/interim/METREF/cdo.log           # status=processed / failed per file
grep -c "status=processed" data/interim/METREF/cdo.log

One *_processed.nc per raw file, and no status=failed lines in cdo.log.
The grid matches code/preprocess_utils/grid.txt.
Value ranges are close to the raw file’s; the number of missing values is plausible (ocean, masks).

Likely cause

Wrong variable

Real masks (sea, clouds, retrieval QA)

title: B · Download and preprocess
text:
Method notes

Regridding never adds detail: a finer target grid only interpolates the source.
Bilinear smooths continuous fields (extremes can shrink); nearest keeps categories but looks blocky.
Degree cells shrink with latitude (0.05° ≈ 5.5 km at the equator, ≈ 5.3 km at 15° N in longitude).
Record product version, AOI, grid, remap method and software versions with your results.

A · Setup B · Download & preprocess C · Zarr cube D · Explore

title: C · Build the Zarr cube
text:
A · Setup B · Download & preprocess C · Zarr cube D · Explore
code/03_build_zarr_cube.py turns the interim NetCDF files of one product into a single Zarr v3 store: one time axis, one grid, compressed chunks grouped into shards, with consolidated metadata so it opens instantly.

title: C · Build the Zarr cube
text:
1 · Preview the plan (dry run)
Always look before you write. --dry-run opens the files lazily and prints what would be built:
uv run python code/03_build_zarr_cube.py --input data/interim/METREF --dry-run
Profile          : map
Files            : 30  (…201506010000_processed.nc … …201506300000_processed.nc)
Variables        : METREF, quality_flag
Dimensions       : {'time': 30, 'lat': 91, 'lon': 121}
Time range       : 2015-06-01 → 2015-06-30
Inner chunk      : {'time': 1, 'lat': 91, 'lon': 121}  (~43.0 KB raw each)
Shard            : {'time': 10, 'lat': 91, 'lon': 121}
Per variable     : 30 inner chunks in 3 shard object(s)
Uncompressed size: 1.9 MB
Output           : …/data/zarr/metref_cube.zarr

Dry run: nothing written.

title: C · Build the Zarr cube
text:
2 · Build
uv run python code/03_build_zarr_cube.py --input data/interim/METREF
…
Validation OK    : first/last time steps match the interim NetCDF
Valid fraction   : METREF=95.9%, quality_flag=100.0%
Stored size      : 841.8 KB in 15 files (compression ≈ 2.3× vs 1.9 MB in memory)
Done in 3.3s → …/data/zarr/metref_cube.zarr
What happens, in order:


Open lazily. All *_processed.nc files under --input are opened with xarray + Dask, concatenated along time in file-name order (no coordinate re-alignment — they share one grid, which is verified against the last file).


Plan chunks. Inner chunks and shards come from the --profile; shards are rounded to whole multiples of the inner chunk (a Zarr v3 requirement) and clamped to the data size.


Write safely. Dask writes whole shards in parallel to <output>.tmp. Stale NetCDF encodings are dropped; provenance (zarr_cube_* attributes) is added.


Validate, then swap. The first and last time steps are compared value-by-value with their source files. Only then is the old cube replaced — a failed run never destroys a working cube.

title: C · Build the Zarr cube
text:
4 · Explore the chunk layout
Chunks decide which questions are cheap. A single-date map should touch few chunks; a long time series at one pixel should too — but one layout cannot make both minimal. Change the cube size and profile and watch what each query has to read.


  
  
    --profile
    mapbalancedtimeseries
  
  
    time steps: 365
    lat cells: 300
    lon cells: 400
  
  
  
  


Rules of thumb

Aim for inner chunks of roughly 100 KB – a few MB (uncompressed). Tiny chunks mean many requests; huge chunks mean reading data you do not need.
Map-heavy work (daily maps, animations): --profile map. Time-series-heavy work (pixel/zone trends, anomalies): --profile timeseries. Unsure: balanced.
Shards reduce the number of files/objects (important on laptops, HPC and object storage); they do not change what is decompressed.
Benchmark your real queries before scaling up — these profiles are starting points, not optima.

title: C · Build the Zarr cube
text:
5 · Open the cube
import xarray as xr

1ds = xr.open_zarr("data/zarr/metref_cube.zarr")
print(ds)
2print(ds.METREF.encoding["chunks"], ds.METREF.encoding["shards"])

3day_map = ds.METREF.sel(time="2015-06-15")
4series  = ds.METREF.sel(lon=-16.4, lat=14.5, method="nearest")
5monthly = ds.METREF.resample(time="1MS").sum()
day_map.plot(); series.plot()

1

Consolidated metadata → a single read, whatever the number of chunks. Nothing is loaded yet.

2

The layout you chose, stored with the data.

3

Select by label (date), not by file.

4

Nearest grid cell to a coordinate — check that it is the cell you expect.

5

Any xarray operation works lazily; only the touched chunks are read when you plot or .compute().


The notebooks in D · Explore build on this with validation, comparison plots and the reusable code/plot_utils functions.

title: C · Build the Zarr cube
text:
7 · Scaling beyond the sample
For a larger region or many years: benchmark a representative subset (runtime, peak memory, stored size, read speed of your real queries), then process in time batches and grow the cube with --append. For very large areas split into grid-aligned tiles with a remapping margin, write each to its own store or to non-overlapping Zarr regions, and keep a manifest so only failed batches are re-run.
